clue.text: Heather offers article on Terry Pratchett work

indicators.note: in a down clue one piece written on another sits below it, so the article follows the novel

parts.note: Eric is a Discworld novel by Terry Pratchett
a is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A gardener's heather plant is offered alongside a Discworld book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' in a down clue puts A below ERIC. Erica is the botanical genus of heaths and heathers.
explanation.definitionFit: Erica is the plant genus that includes the heaths, the shrubs commonly called heather.

clue.text: "I remember Port Selda" (on the up-line)

indicators.note: a down clue is read upwards, and a railway's up-line runs the other way, so the words are turned backwards

explanation.surface: A quoted railway memory of a station called Port Selda, as seen from the up-line.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation is the opening of Edward Thomas's poem 'Adlestrop' ('Yes. I remember Adlestrop'), about a train halting at a Cotswold station; 'on the up-line' turns PORTSELDA upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The poem titled with this station name opens with the words 'Yes. I remember' followed by the name, so the clue quotes its line.

clue.text: The quest for Snow

parts.note: Snow here is the novelist C. P. Snow, whose 1934 novel has a title meaning a hunt or quest, not a hunt for snowfall

explanation.surface: An expedition sets out in search of snowy weather.
explanation.definitionFit: C. P. Snow's early novel about a scientist is titled with this word for a hunt or quest.

clue.text: Illuminating Hamilton work

definitions.meaning: lighting by burning coal gas, as street lamps once were
Patrick Hamilton wrote the 1938 thriller play ...

explanation.definitionFit: Lamps fuelled by gas lit Victorian streets, and Patrick Hamilton's stage thriller about a manipulative husband takes that lamp for its title.

clue.text: Vague, restful " tab possibly identifies French writer

indicators.note: possibly says the letters of these three words might be arranged into something else

explanation.surface: A vague, relaxed tab supposedly pins down a writer from France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' rearranges VAGUE, RESTFUL and TAB (fifteen letters) into the novelist's full name; the stray quotation mark is a print mark.
explanation.definitionFit: The author of Madame Bovary was a nineteenth-century novelist from Rouen.

clue.text: Scoffer at crime by Alice Thomas Ellis

indicators.note: at here means placed next to, so the crime word stands beside the scoffer

parts.note: a sin is a wrongdoing or offence
one who scoffs food is an eater

explanation.surface: Someone who mocks crime appears in a book by Alice Thomas Ellis.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scoffer' reads as one who mocks but means one who eats greedily. A sin-eater was a person paid to eat food over a corpse and so take on the dead person's sins.
explanation.definitionFit: Alice Thomas Ellis's first novel, published in 1977, is titled The Sin Eater.

clue.text: MacDonald's princess upsets northern Eire

indicators.note: upsets means the letters are knocked over and set down in a new order

explanation.surface: A fairy-tale princess causes upset in the north of Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upsets' rearranges N and EIRE. George MacDonald's The Princess and the Goblin has a princess of this name.
explanation.definitionFit: The heroine of George MacDonald's The Princess and the Goblin and The Princess and Curdie bears this name.

clue.text: Welsh poet seen to rhyme "push" inaccurately

indicators.note: inaccurately says the letters of the two words are set down wrongly, in a new order

explanation.surface: A poet from Wales is spotted making a careless rhyme on the word push.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inaccurately' rearranges RHYME and PUSH. Emyr Humphreys was a Welsh novelist and poet.
explanation.definitionFit: Emyr Humphreys, born in Flintshire, wrote poetry and novels of Welsh life.

clue.text: Novelist friend of Lawrence presents archetypal schoolboy and another lad

parts.note: William Brown of Richmal Crompton's Just William stories is the classic English schoolboy
a son is a boy

explanation.surface: A novelist who knew Lawrence is introduced alongside a famous schoolboy and a second boy.
explanation.walkthrough: Henry Williamson, author of Tarka the Otter, was a friend of T. E. Lawrence. William is the scruffy hero of Richmal Crompton's British children's books.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry Williamson corresponded with T. E. Lawrence, who was riding to visit him when he crashed his motorcycle.

clue.text: Part of item made by novelist

indicators.note: part of says only a stretch of the following words is wanted, running across them

explanation.surface: A piece of something produced by a writer of novels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Part of' takes the letters running across 'itEM MAde'; Jane Austen is the novelist.
explanation.definitionFit: Jane Austen's 1815 novel takes its title from its matchmaking heroine Miss Woodhouse.

clue.text: Odysseus heard that she played ball

definitions.text: Odysseus heard that she played ball

parts.words: Odysseus heard that she played ball
parts.note: in the Odyssey the shipwrecked hero is woken by the cries of a Phaeacian princess and her maids playing ball on the shore

explanation.walkthrough: 'heard' is not a sound-alike signal: in Book 6 of the Odyssey the shouts of the ball game wake the castaway hero.
explanation.definitionFit: The Phaeacian princess, daughter of King Alcinous, finds the washed-up hero while playing ball with her handmaids.

clue.text: She who was featured in fiction

definitions.text: She who was featured in fiction

parts.words: She who was featured in fiction
parts.note: Rider Haggard's novel She has an immortal queen known as She-who-must-be-obeyed

explanation.walkthrough: 'She' reads as a pronoun but is the title of Rider Haggard's 1887 novel, whose ageless queen is called She-who-must-be-obeyed.
explanation.definitionFit: The ageless queen of Kôr in Rider Haggard's novel She carries this name.

clue.text: Emperor destroys Hamelin plague

indicators.note: destroys means the word is wrecked and its letters set up in a new order

parts.note: the Pied Piper rid the town of Hamelin of a plague of rats

explanation.surface: A ruler wipes out the pests that infested Hamelin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'destroys' rearranges RATS, the plague the Pied Piper cleared from Hamelin, into the Russian ruler's title.
explanation.definitionFit: Russia's rulers took the imperial title, derived from the Latin Caesar.

clue.text: Two states support dynasty in earthly paradise

indicators.note: in a down clue the supporting pieces sit underneath the piece they hold up

parts.note: the Shang dynasty ruled ancient China
RI is the postal abbreviation for the US state Rhode Island
LA is the postal abbreviation for the US state Louisiana

explanation.surface: Two nations prop up a ruling house within an earthly heaven.
explanation.walkthrough: 'support' puts RI and LA below SHANG in this down clue. The paradise is the hidden valley of James Hilton's Lost Horizon.
explanation.definitionFit: James Hilton's Lost Horizon invented a hidden Himalayan valley of peace and long life, now a byword for utopia.

clue.text: A chapel for Scrooge

definitions.meaning: the Hebrew name meaning stone of help was often given to Nonconformist chapels in Britain
Dickens's miser in A Christmas Carol has this first name

explanation.definitionFit: Many Welsh and English Nonconformist chapels bear this biblical name, which is also the forename of Dickens's miser.

clue.text: Foundling in strange passé epic

indicators.note: strange means the letters of the words are arranged in an unfamiliar way

explanation.surface: An abandoned child turns up in an odd, old-fashioned epic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strange' rearranges PASSE and EPIC. The child is the foundling of George Eliot's Silas Marner.
explanation.definitionFit: In George Eliot's Silas Marner the weaver raises a toddler who wanders into his cottage, the secret daughter of Godfrey Cass.

clue.text: Charles Dibdin's renegade

definitions.meaning: Charles Dibdin wrote the 1773 musical play The ...
a renegade abandons his side or cause

explanation.definitionFit: A renegade forsakes his cause like a soldier who runs off, and Dibdin's comic opera has that title.

clue.text: One of several Commonwealth poets said to be coming men

definitions.meaning: Thomas ..., Roy ... and Wilfred ... were poets from Scotland, South Africa and Canada
the Scottish song The ... Are Coming describes the clan marching

explanation.definitionFit: Poets of this surname came from Scotland, South Africa and Canada, and the Scottish song says the clansmen of this name are coming.

clue.text: Job at Bukowski's office

definitions.meaning: a job is a position or appointment
Charles Bukowski's first novel is titled ... Office

explanation.definitionFit: A post is a position of employment, and the word comes before 'Office' in Bukowski's novel title.

clue.text: 12 must be

parts.note: the answer to 12 across is the queen called She-who-must-be followed by the missing word

explanation.walkthrough: 12 across is Haggard's queen, whose title 'She-who-must-be-...' is completed by this word.
explanation.definitionFit: Haggard's queen demands complete compliance, and her title ends with the past participle of comply's synonym.

clue.text: Appellation given to Scipio, acquiring silver and terribly mean

parts.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver

indicators.note: terribly says the letters of the following word are disturbed into a new order

explanation.surface: A Roman general's title is said to include silver and real meanness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'terribly' rearranges MEAN. Scipio earned the extra name Africanus for defeating Carthage.
explanation.definitionFit: An agname or agnomen is an extra name added by Romans for a feat, like Scipio's Africanus.

clue.text: He may have ruled in Hanley's 1978 subject matter

definitions.text: He may have ruled in Hanley's 1978 subject matter

parts.words: He may have ruled in Hanley's 1978 subject matter
parts.note: James Hanley's 1978 novel takes a realm as its title, and the person described is one who would have reigned over such a realm

explanation.walkthrough: James Hanley's last novel (1978) is titled with the word for a monarch's realm, preceded by the article; the ruler, with that article, opens the book's title.
explanation.definitionFit: A monarch is the one who rules a realm, which Hanley's title names.

clue.text: Broadly embracing title of Mount's Pacific Tale

definitions.meaning: an all-covering term or organisation is described this way
Ferdinand Mount's 1994 novel is subtitled A Pacific Tale

explanation.definitionFit: An all-inclusive heading shelters many items like a parasol, and Ferdinand Mount's novel of Fiji bears that title.

clue.text: Yeats and Eliot published such poems

definitions.text: Yeats and Eliot published such poems

parts.words: Yeats and Eliot published such poems
parts.note: both poets issued a collection of their subsequent, more recent work under this adjective

explanation.walkthrough: Yeats issued Later Poems in 1922; the clue asks for the word describing a poet's subsequent output.
explanation.definitionFit: Poems from a subsequent period of a poet's career are gathered in collections with this title.

clue.text: US soldiers in filmed French novel

parts.note: GI is slang for an American soldier
GI again, the plural giving two of them

explanation.surface: American troops appear in a screen adaptation of a book from France.
explanation.walkthrough: The plural 'soldiers' supplies two GIs. Colette's novella became the 1958 musical film.
explanation.definitionFit: Colette's 1944 novella about a Parisian girl trained as a courtesan became a Lerner and Loewe musical film.

clue.text: Haydn tests composition a dramatic epic

indicators.note: a composition is something put together, so the letters are assembled afresh

explanation.surface: Haydn tests a piece of music that is a grand theatrical epic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'composition' looks musical beside Haydn but rearranges HAYDN and TESTS. Thomas Hardy's verse drama of the Napoleonic wars is the epic.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Hardy's three-part verse play on the Napoleonic Wars is an epic drama meant for mental performance.

clue.text: Fiercely ambitious queen of a Juno sort

definitions.text: Fiercely ambitious queen of a Juno sort

parts.words: Fiercely ambitious queen of a Juno sort
parts.note: Henry VI's warlike consort came from Anjou, whose letters are those of 'a Juno' sorted

explanation.walkthrough: 'of a Juno sort' looks like a comparison with the Roman queen of the gods but rearranges A JUNO into ANJOU, the home of Henry VI's queen.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry VI's wife, from Anjou, led the Lancastrian armies in the Wars of the Roses and is a fierce figure in Shakespeare.

clue.text: Situated by O'Neill beneath doomed trees

definitions.text: Situated by O'Neill beneath doomed trees

parts.words: Situated by O'Neill beneath doomed trees
parts.note: Eugene O'Neill's 1924 play places a longing under the elms, trees doomed by Dutch elm disease

explanation.walkthrough: O'Neill's play is Desire Under the Elms; elms are 'doomed' because Dutch elm disease killed most of them.
explanation.definitionFit: Eugene O'Neill's tragedy of a New England farm is titled with this longing set under the elms.
